name: Hipparchus and the epicycle theory (toward the Ptolemaic system)
plain_explanation: Hipparchus, called by the historian Heath 'the greatest astronomer of antiquity,' rejected Aristarchus's sun-centered theory and instead refined an alternative geocentric model using 'epicycles' -- circles moving on circles -- which later astronomers developed into the complex, earth-centered Ptolemaic system that dominated astronomy for over a thousand years.
precise_definition: Hipparchus's (fl. 161-126 BC) adoption and improvement of the epicycle theory (originally invented by Apollonius, fl. ca. 220 BC) as a geocentric alternative to Aristarchus's heliocentric hypothesis, combined with genuinely major achievements -- the first systematic trigonometry, discovery of the precession of the equinoxes, a highly accurate lunar month estimate, improved sun/moon distance estimates, and a catalogue of 850 fixed stars -- whose cumulative authority caused the heliocentric hypothesis to be set aside until Copernicus.
why_it_mattered: Hipparchus's work, later systematized by Ptolemy (fl. mid-second century AD) into what became known as the Ptolemaic system, was largely responsible for the 'general rejection' of Aristarchus's correct heliocentric hypothesis for roughly seventeen centuries.
historical_origin: Developed by Hipparchus, building on Apollonius's earlier invention of epicycles.
examples: Hipparchus estimated the length of the lunar month with an error of less than one second.
He catalogued eight hundred and fifty fixed stars, giving their latitude and longitude.
competing_positions: Aristarchus's and Seleucus's heliocentric hypothesis, which the epicycle tradition displaced for the remainder of antiquity.
influence_on_later_thinkers: Developed by Ptolemy into the 'Ptolemaic system,' the dominant astronomical model in the West and the Islamic world until Copernicus.
